title: How Today's Students Are Different And What It Means For You
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Reflecting on 27 years of teaching, Linsin argues that while the fundamentals of effective classroom management haven't changed, one notable shift has: today's students are more responsive than ever to teachers who are consistently kind and pleasant, and simultaneously far less tolerant of negative methods like lecturing, scolding, and glaring. He warns that even brief or occasional negative methods now carry an outsized cost, causing students to disengage, misbehave covertly, or quietly dislike the teacher, and that many teachers struggle with classroom management precisely because they cling to these outdated habits without realizing it. His prescription is straightforward: rely exclusively on a well-taught classroom management plan to hold students accountable, abandon any negative methods entirely, and lean into ordinary kindness—smiling, saying hello, being gentle—since students today are forgiving of past mistakes as long as the change is genuine and sustained.
points: The fundamentals of classroom management remain unchanged after 27 years, but student responsiveness to teacher demeanor has shifted.
Today's students are more affected by small acts of consistent kindness than in past decades.
Even occasional negative methods like lecturing or glaring now carry a disproportionately high cost in student trust.
Many teachers struggle with classroom management because they don't realize their own negative habits are the underlying cause.
Students are described as forgiving and forgetful, meaning teachers can reset a damaged dynamic quickly by committing to consistent kindness.
quotes: Students today are more appreciative, more influenced, and more affected by teachers who are consistently kind and pleasant.
Simple, day-after-day kindness is the one sure way to gain leverage and influence with any group of students, no matter how challenging.
Today’s students are savvy and worldly and have a deep conviction that negative methods of classroom management are not okay with them.
The hard truth is that there is no longer a place for lecturing, scolding, glaring, and the like in an effective teacher’s toolkit.

So many teachers are flailing in the dark, trying out this strategy and that one, never realizing that the reason they struggle with classroom management is that their students privately dislike them.
The good news is that kids are incredibly forgiving—and forgetful.
